newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan coffee prices seen continuing to rally.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan coffee prices seen continuing to rally.

text.p: Kenyan coffee prices will continue to rally in the near term after touching highest levels since 1994, due to the global shortage of mild arabica coffees, traders and industry officials said on Wednesday.

They said prices were a major incentive for farmers to improve production, threatened in 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) by coffee berry disease in June to July last year and drought in December to March this year.

If good weather prevails, coffee authorities are already speaking of a harvest of 100,000-110,000 tonnes in 1997/98. They say farmers now keep up to 80 percent of the sale prices realised at auctions and will feel very encouraged by current prices.
At the weekly export auction on Tuesday, quality coffees gained up to $30 per 50 kg (110.25 lb) on speculative buying.
Premium grade ABs averaged $439 per 50-kg compared to $403 last week while grade AAs sold at $451 from $417. Grade PBs averaged $450 from $402, according to data issued by Kenya Coffee Auctions Ltd.

Traders in Nairobi put sale prices even higher, at between $472 and $540 FAQ (Fair Average Quality) for AAs and between $462 and $520 for ABs. This compared to $422 and 465 FAQ for AAs and $410 and $474 per 50 kg for ABs last week.
In February, AAs ranged around $239 FAQ while ABs were around $238, traders and industry leaders said.
The latest rally extended gains made since the beginning of the year on speculative buying spurred by tight world supplies which are seen persisting through the year.
Traders were optimistic that prices would remain firm on account of a lack of sufficient quality washed arabica coffees in the second half of the calendar year.

"We can safely say that (Kenyan) coffee prices will remain stable in the near future because there is a big demand for Kenyan coffee, normally used for blending," said Kenya Coffee Board Public Relations Manager Paul Kivila.
"This time, only an average of three grades sold below $400 compared to last week when only two grades sold above the $400 mark," Kivila told Reuters. There are 10 grades auctioned.
Supermarkets said they were transferring the high cost of coffee directly to consumers. Kenyans consume only around five percent of the 80,000-100,000 tonnes of coffee they produce.

"In less than three months, prices (of coffee) have gone up by 20-50 percent on average from the supplier to the consumer," said Vimal Shah, a director at Nakumatt Holdings Ltd, Nairobi's leading supermarket chain, which sells an average of 5,000 tonnes of coffee a year.
The failure of seasonal short rains in key growing areas between October and December and subsequent drought that persisted to late March has adversely affected the crop.

Already, farmers harvesting the early fly crop say coffee beans are not well developed and appear withered. Many of the beans are broken. That spells problems with quality at auctions before the end of the season.
The coffee board estimates 1996/97 production will at most reach 80,000 tonnes compared with 97,575 in 1995/96 and 95,806 in 1994/95.
The coffee board sold 35,480 60-kg bags of coffee compared ot 36,456 bags sold last week. In Kenya coffee is measured in 50-kg bags but sold in 60-kg bags. --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261.
